title: Samsung and SK Hynix Ink $950 Billion Memory Chip Deals with US Tech Giants
excerpt: South Korea's semiconductor champions commit to massive long-term supply partnerships with Nvidia, Broadcom, and other AI leaders during President Lee's San Francisco summit.
body:
• SK Hynix will supply $750 billion in memory chips to U.S. companies including Nvidia; Samsung Electronics commits $200 billion to Broadcom.
  • Nvidia and SK Group unveiled a separate $500 billion-plus initiative covering AI data centers and next-generation HBM4 memory.
  • SK Telecom plans a 2-gigawatt data center powered by Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips and SK Hynix HBM4, due online in 2027.
  • The deals follow South Korea's $576 billion national semiconductor investment plan announced in June 2026.

South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have signed memory chip supply partnerships with major U.S. technology companies worth a combined $950 billion, according to South Korea's presidential policy adviser Kim Yong-beom.

The deals, announced Saturday at an AI summit hosted by South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in San Francisco, break down into two pillars: SK Hynix will supply $750 billion in memory chips to U.S. firms including Nvidia, while Samsung Electronics has committed $200 billion in chip supply to Broadcom, Kim told a briefing, according to Reuters.

A San Francisco Summit With Global Stakes

President Lee convened the summit as part of a broader diplomatic push to position South Korea as a linchpin in the global AI supply chain. About 150 executives, investors, researchers, and startup founders attended, Reuters reported.

https://x.com/PankajK250/status/2080969856728387844

Lee met individually with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Broadcom CEO Hock Tan before joining the wider forum. On the Korean side, Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung, and Naver founder Lee Hae-jin were present.

Lee unveiled what he called a "San Francisco AI Declaration," outlining South Korea's ambitions for deeper technological cooperation with the United States.

"I'd like to present a vision for the future of AI and propose global cooperation to make it happen."

— Lee Jae Myung, President of South Korea

Nvidia-SK Group: $500 Billion and a 2-Gigawatt Data Center

On the sidelines, Nvidia and SK Group announced a separate $500 billion-plus initiative spanning large-scale AI data centers and next-generation memory technology, according to Reuters.

Under the agreement, SK Telecom will build a 2-gigawatt data center powered by Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips and SK Hynix's HBM4 high-bandwidth memory chips. The facility is expected to come online in 2027.

SK Group Chairman Chey said AI customers are demanding far more memory than previously anticipated, citing recent conversations with Nvidia, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Broadcom.

"I wouldn't be surprised if, the next time I see [Huang], he'll tell me those figures were too low and say, 'I want more.'"

— Chey Tae-won, Chairman, SK Group

Chey added that Broadcom CEO Hock Tan told him his company's memory demand was likely to surpass available supply. OpenAI, meanwhile, has urged SK to supply chips directly to the ChatGPT maker, Chey said.

Anthropic Joins the Memory Rush

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei confirmed at the summit that the AI startup had signed supply deals with both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, though he did not disclose terms. In May, Anthropic raised funding at a post-money valuation of $965 billion, naming Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron as partners whose technologies play a critical role in its chip supply chain, Reuters reported.

Chey also said Anthropic was developing its own "computing power," possibly referring to a Reuters report that the AI lab is exploring the possibility of designing custom chips — a move that would underscore the sector's urgency to address a worsening chip shortage.

Building on a $576 Billion National Bet

The San Francisco deals cap a month of aggressive semiconductor moves by Seoul. In late June, President Lee unveiled three state-driven mega-projects anchored by Samsung and SK Hynix, totaling more than $576 billion in investment. That plan includes $518 billion for four new memory fabrication sites in South Korea's southwest, $52 billion for an HBM packaging hub, and $356 billion for AI data centers to be built by companies including SK, GS, and Naver through 2035.

"Semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers are the triple axis for South Korea's next industrial era," Lee said at the June announcement, calling 2026 the year the country must establish itself as an "irreplaceable" industrial power.

What It Means for the Diaspora

Indian-origin engineers and executives hold senior roles across the U.S. tech companies at the center of these deals — Nvidia, Broadcom, and the major AI labs. The expansion of semiconductor supply chains between the U.S. and South Korea is likely to drive hiring in chip design, AI infrastructure, and data center engineering, sectors where Indian professionals are heavily represented in Silicon Valley and beyond.

What's Next

President Lee is set to attend a meeting Saturday between South Korea's National Pension Service — the world's third-largest pension fund — and U.S. venture capital firms to encourage investment in Korean startups. He then heads to South America for regional summits. The chip supply deals still need to be formalized into binding contracts, and industry watchers will be tracking whether the headline figures translate into firm purchase orders as the global AI buildout accelerates through 2027 and beyond.
